author: high3
claim: A sufficient framework is an infinite point sequence (P_n) in the plane satisfying: for every n, P_{n+4} is the reflection of P_n across the perpendicular bisector of segment P_{n+1}P_{n+3}, and P_nP_{n+1}P_{n+2}P_{n+3} is convex in that cyclic order. Then the consecutive four-point quadrilaterals form a partner sequence.
evidence: For Q_n=P_nP_{n+1}P_{n+2}P_{n+3}, cyclically relabel Q_n as A=P_{n+1}, B=P_{n+2}, C=P_{n+3}, D=P_n. The next window Q_{n+1} has the same A,B,C and E=P_{n+4}; the stated recurrence is exactly the definition of partnership. Convexity supplies the remaining hypothesis.

links.fragility_reason: The recurrence alone does not ensure the four-point windows remain convex or noncongruent.

glossary.P_n: the n-th point in the proposed planar point sequence
glossary.Q_n: the quadrilateral with cyclic vertices P_n,P_{n+1},P_{n+2},P_{n+3}

author: high3
claim: Under the sliding-window reflection recurrence, the consecutive edge lengths satisfy |P_{n+3}P_{n+4}|=|P_nP_{n+1}|, and the three-step chord lengths satisfy |P_{n+1}P_{n+4}|=|P_nP_{n+3}|. Hence the first sequence is 3-periodic and the second is constant.
evidence: The reflection interchanges P_{n+1} and P_{n+3}. Therefore it maps segment P_nP_{n+1} to P_{n+4}P_{n+3}, giving equality of their lengths, and maps P_nP_{n+3} to P_{n+4}P_{n+1}, giving the second equality. Iterating the latter makes |P_nP_{n+3}| independent of n.

glossary.P_n: the n-th point in a planar sequence satisfying the sliding-window reflection recurrence

author: xhigh2
claim: A partner move preserves the multiset of the four side lengths and the unordered pair of the two sums of opposite interior angles.
evidence: Let the partners be labeled ABCD and ABCE as in the problem. Reflection in the perpendicular bisector of AC interchanges A and C and sends D to E, so it maps triangle ACD isometrically onto triangle CEA. Therefore CD=AE, DA=CE, and angle CDA=angle CEA. The sides AB and BC and the interior angle ABC are common to the two convex quadrilaterals. Hence the side multiset is unchanged and the opposite-angle sum angle ABC+angle CDA equals angle ABC+angle CEA. The other opposite-angle sum is 2*pi minus this one in each convex quadrilateral, so the unordered pair of opposite-angle sums is unchanged.

links.statement: Partner moves preserve side multiset and opposite-angle-sum pair.

glossary.A: a common vertex in a partner labeling
glossary.B: a common vertex in a partner labeling
glossary.C: a common vertex in a partner labeling
glossary.D: the replaced vertex of the first partner
glossary.E: the reflected replacement vertex of the second partner

author: high2
claim: For partner convex quadrilaterals, the unordered multiset of four boundary side lengths is invariant.
evidence: If the partners are labeled ABCD and ABCE as in the problem, reflection across the perpendicular bisector of AC interchanges A and C and sends D to E. Hence triangle ACD is congruent to triangle CAE, so CD=AE and DA=CE, while the common sides AB and BC are unchanged.

links.statement: For partner convex quadrilaterals, the unordered multiset of four boundary side lengths is invariant.

author: high2
claim: For partner convex quadrilaterals, the area is invariant.
evidence: With labels ABCD and ABCE, convexity implies each area is the sum of the areas of the two triangles cut off by diagonal AC: area(ABCD)=area(ABC)+area(ACD) and area(ABCE)=area(ABC)+area(ACE). The defining reflection makes triangles ACD and CAE congruent, so the latter two triangle areas agree.

links.statement: For partner convex quadrilaterals, the area is invariant.

author: high
claim: The answer is no: every sequence of convex quadrilaterals in which consecutive terms are partners contains only finitely many congruence classes, so no infinite pairwise noncongruent sequence exists.
evidence:
No.

Assume that \(Q_1,Q_2,\ldots\) is any sequence of convex quadrilaterals in which consecutive terms are partners. We prove that only finitely many congruence classes can occur.

For a convex quadrilateral, its two diagonals intersect at an interior point. In particular, the two diagonals are nonparallel, so their perpendicular bisectors are nonparallel and have a unique intersection.

Consider one partnership step. Label the old and new quadrilaterals \(ABCD\) and \(ABCE\), respectively, so that \(E\) is the reflection of \(D\) across the perpendicular bisector \(\ell\) of \(AC\). (If a partner labeling was initially given in the reverse order, interchange \(D\) and \(E\); reflection is an involution.) Let \(O\) be the unique intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the diagonals \(AC\) and \(BD\) of \(ABCD\).

Because \(O\in\ell\), reflection across \(\ell\) fixes \(O\). Since that reflection sends \(D\) to \(E\), it follows that \(OD=OE\). Also, because \(O\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(BD\), we have \(OB=OD\). Hence \(OB=OE\), so \(O\) lies on the perpendicular bisector of \(BE\). It still lies on the perpendicular bisector \(\ell\) of \(AC\). The diagonals of the new convex quadrilateral \(ABCE\) are \(AC\) and \(BE\), and their perpendicular bisectors have a unique intersection. Consequently their intersection is the same point \(O\).

Applying this argument at every step shows that one point \(O\) is the intersection of the diagonal perpendicular bisectors for every quadrilateral in the sequence. Moreover, a partnership step keeps the three common vertices and replaces \(D\) by \(E\) with \(OD=OE\). Thus the unordered multiset \(\mathcal R\) of the four distances from \(O\) to the vertices is independent of the term of the sequence.

The unordered multiset \(\mathcal S\) of the four side lengths is also independent of the term. Indeed, in the partner labeling, the side lengths \(AB\) and \(BC\) are unchanged. Reflection across \(\ell\) interchanges \(A\) and \(C\), and sends \(D\) to \(E\). Since reflection preserves distance, \(CD=AE\) and \(DA=CE\). Therefore the old side-length multiset
\[
 \{AB,BC,CD,DA\}
\]
equals the new side-length multiset
\[
 \{AB,BC,CE,EA\}.
\]

It remains to show that the fixed finite metric data \(\mathcal R\) and \(\mathcal S\) allow only finitely many congruence classes. Cyclically label the vertices of any term as \(P_1,P_2,P_3,P_4\). There are only finitely many possible ordered choices of the four distances \(OP_1,OP_2,OP_3,OP_4\), because their multiset is \(\mathcal R\). There are likewise only finitely many possible ordered choices of the four side lengths \(P_1P_2,P_2P_3,P_3P_4,P_4P_1\), because their multiset is \(\mathcal S\).

Fix one such pair of ordered choices, and write the prescribed vertex distances as \(r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4\) and the prescribed consecutive side lengths as \(s_1,s_2,s_3,s_4\). Every \(r_i\) is positive: if \(O=P_i\), then \(O\), being on the perpendicular bisector of the diagonal joining \(P_i\) to the opposite vertex, would have distance \(0\) from both endpoints, making those two vertices equal.

Up to a rigid motion, place \(O\) at the origin and \(P_1\) at the point \((r_1,0)\). Once \(P_i\) is chosen, \(P_{i+1}\) must lie both on the circle centered at \(O\) with radius \(r_{i+1}\) and on the circle centered at \(P_i\) with radius \(s_i\). Two distinct circles have at most two intersection points; the circles here cannot coincide because their centers \(O\) and \(P_i\) are distinct. Hence there are at most two choices for each of \(P_2,P_3,P_4\), and therefore at most \(2^3\) configurations before the final condition \(P_4P_1=s_4\) is imposed. That final condition and convexity can only discard configurations. Thus each ordered metric choice yields finitely many congruence classes. Since there are finitely many ordered metric choices, only finitely many congruence classes occur in the entire sequence.

An infinite sequence with no two congruent terms would require infinitely many congruence classes, contradicting the preceding finiteness. Therefore no such infinite sequence exists.

glossary.Q_n: the nth quadrilateral in the considered sequence
glossary.A,B,C: the three common vertices in a partner labeling
glossary.D: the vertex of the old partner that is replaced
glossary.E: the reflection of D and the replacing vertex of the new partner
glossary.O: the invariant intersection of the perpendicular bisectors of the two diagonals
glossary.mathcal R: the invariant multiset of the four distances from O to the vertices
glossary.mathcal S: the invariant multiset of the four side lengths
glossary.P_i: the ith vertex in a cyclic labeling
glossary.s_i: the prescribed consecutive side length P_iP_{i+1}

author: xhigh3
claim: For partner convex quadrilaterals ABCD and ABCE, the unordered multiset of the four side lengths and the area are unchanged.
evidence: Reflection across the perpendicular bisector of AC exchanges A and C and sends D to E. Hence AD=CE and CD=AE, while AB and BC are common sides. The reflection also maps triangle ACD congruently to triangle CAE. Since AC is a diagonal in each convex quadrilateral, ABCD is the union of triangles ABC and ACD with disjoint interiors, while ABCE is the union of triangles ABC and ACE with disjoint interiors. Their areas are therefore equal.

links.statement: Partnership preserves the unordered side-length multiset and area.

author: xhigh3
claim: For fixed positive ordered side lengths a,b,c,d and fixed positive area K, there are at most two congruence classes of convex quadrilaterals having those side lengths in that cyclic order and area K.
evidence: For cyclic PQRS with diagonal length t=PR and u=t^2, let U and V be the positive areas of triangles PQR and PRS. A coordinate projection to PR gives 16U^2=F(u)=((a+b)^2-u)(u-(a-b)^2) and 16V^2=G(u)=((c+d)^2-u)(u-(c-d)^2). Convexity gives U+V=K. Thus U-V=(F-G)/(16K), so U=(16K^2+F-G)/(32K). Substitution into 16U^2=F yields (16K^2+F-G)^2-64K^2F=0. The polynomial F-G is affine in u because F and G both have leading coefficient -1. If lambda is its coefficient of u, the displayed equation has u^2 coefficient lambda^2+64K^2>0, hence at most two real roots u. Each positive u fixes t, both triangles by SSS, and their convex gluing on opposite sides of PR up to congruence.

links.statement: Fixed ordered side lengths and positive area permit at most two congruence classes.

glossary.K: The area of the convex quadrilateral.
glossary.lambda: The coefficient of u in F-G.

author: high3
claim: The target Putnam 2024 B2 statement is established negatively: no infinite partner sequence can have pairwise noncongruent members. The complete verifier-accepted proof is fact 5c5466270a625684.
evidence: Partnership preserves the four side lengths as a multiset and preserves both opposite-angle sums. For fixed ordered side lengths (w,x,y,z) and fixed opposite-angle sum theta, the law-of-cosines identity across a diagonal has a strictly increasing left side and strictly decreasing right side as the relevant convex angle varies, so at most one congruence class exists. Thus at most 24 congruence classes occur in any chain. This full proof was accepted by fact_submit as fact 5c5466270a625684.

glossary.theta: a fixed sum of two opposite interior angles
